searches.note: Twenty seven searches of a share of twenty eight, one left unspent, none of them the author's. Seven were restricted to a house's own domain (hanzell.com, kistlervineyards.com, williamsselyem.com twice, jordanwinery.com twice, seghesio.com twice, once with sonomawinegrape.org) and are read as primary through their summaries; eleven kept the house's own domain out for an independent second source; one was restricted to four trade papers; the rest went to the open web. One search (Faiveley) was spent largely on a railway company of the same name. No WebFetch was tried.

method: Each record was read with one instruction, refute it: the founding year, the people and their dates, the classification, the grapes, the sites, the making and its months, the drinking window, the serving temperature, the label words, every beat of the story, the cards and the questions; then the house rules (nobody living named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash).

Dates and people went first, then the making, then the picks the plan asked to confirm. Where a search contradicted the record it was set right with its source; where a detail was found in no source of this check it was cut or said with less (the auction of Hanzell's wine, Sebella's malolactic, the respelling of Hanzell, the barns of 1988, the fourth generation of 1983).

Sources whose title or address names a living person, a writer's own site or a score were met among the results (a wine wiki under a writer's first name, two review sites under writers' names, a critic's own site, an interview headed with the name of Hanzell's president, a newsletter note headed with a living winemaker's name, a Press Democrat headline naming a Seghesio vintner) and are cited neither in the fragment nor here, or are cited under a title of this check's own with an address that names no one.
The fragment's own sources were not changed; the sources of this check are listed per change and per record.

tested: Founded 1953, the first vines Chardonnay and Pinot Noir planted that year above Sonoma town: the house's timeline (three acres of each), the Historic Vineyard Society and Prince of Pinot, and the library's year. Confirmed; the land itself was bought in 1943 or 1948 by account, which the record does not give.

James D. Zellerbach (1892 to 1963), a paper industrialist of Crown Zellerbach: Wikipedia and its German counterpart give 17 January 1892 and 3 August 1963; Find a Grave gives the same years. Confirmed.

Ambassador to Italy from 1957: the Office of the Historian and the list of ambassadors give 6 February 1957 to 10 December 1960, the Senate confirming him in January 1957. Confirmed; the first vintage of 1957 is the house's timeline, hedged as its account, with 1956 in some accounts.
The winery of redwood and local stone modelled on the press house of the Clos de Vougeot: the Press Democrat and Prince of Pinot, one calling it a two thirds scale copy. Confirmed.
Small French barrels and temperature controlled steel: the library's why and the house; told as credited. Stands.
The widow's sale to Heitz Cellar: Wikipedia's summary has the bottled and barrelled stock sold to Heitz; no result of this check spoke of an auction. Set right (below).
The Day family in the mid 1960s and the de Brye family in 1975: Wikipedia, Beverage Business and Prince of Pinot give 1965 or 1966 and 1975. Confirmed.

The winemaker hired in 1973 who stayed until 2001: Wine Spectator's and the San Francisco Examiner's obituaries give 1973 to 2001; Decanter and the Sonoma Index-Tribune give 2002, and one account has him made emeritus in 2002. Kept, with the spread open; he died in 2014 and stays described for want of a birth year in two sources.

The making: the house says it uses native yeast, adds no malolactic bacteria and cross flow filters to keep malic acid; Prince of Pinot gives a third fermented in new French barrels and the rest cool in steel for 2007, and thirty per cent barrel fermented with twelve months in thirty per cent new oak for 2010. Confirmed as written (largely steel, a share of new French oak).

The Ambassador's 1953 Vineyard: the Historic Vineyard Society, Prince of Pinot and Wikipedia make it the original block of both Chardonnay and Pinot Noir. The trap set right (below); the library's holdings line stands.
Sebella: the house's page gives stainless steel and six months in neutral French oak, Prince of Pinot one to four year old barrels; nothing on its malolactic. Set right (below).

The rules: no living person named (the de Brye heir, the later owners, the president of the house and every winemaker since 2001 are kept out), no price, no score, nothing volatile, British spelling, no dash. Sound.

The questions: the wine question's malolactic held back against new American oak, skin contact and Sonoma Coast fruit, one right answer; the story question's Heitz Cellar against three Napa houses of the time. Sound once the auction is cut.

changed.was: James D. Zellerbach (1892 to 1963), a paper industrialist who admired the wines of Burgundy, set out to make their like in Sonoma. In 1953 he planted his first vines, Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, on the hillside above Sonoma town, and he named the estate Hanzell for his wife, Hana. The small winery that followed, of redwood and local stone, was modelled on the press house of the Clos de Vougeot, and the first vintage, by the house's account, came in 1957, the year he went to Rome as ambassador to Italy. With his founding winemaker he brought in small barrels of French oak, rare in California then, and temperature controlled fermenters of stainless steel. After Zellerbach died in 1963 his widow sold the stock, and barrels of Hanzell Chardonnay and Pinot Noir went at auction to Heitz Cellar in Napa. The Day family bought and reopened the estate in the mid 1960s, and in 1975 it passed to the de Brye family. A winemaker hired in 1973 stayed until 2001 and held to the firm, long lived style. Hanzell is the estate credited with bringing the small French barrel and the cooled steel tank to California wine.

tested: Founded 1978 on the notion of California wines of site, first vintage 1979: the house's home page and the library; the region record's producers line gives 1979. Confirmed; the tension is in the report.
The Kistler Vineyard bottled on its own since 1986: the house's vineyard page and its notes, with the Ideal Wine Company's account beside them. Confirmed.
Sonoma Valley on the label: the house's own page for the 2019 is titled Kistler Vineyard Chardonnay Sonoma Valley. Confirmed.

A small bowl on the western edge of the Mayacamas, dry farmed, on St George rootstock: the house's vineyard page and its 2023 note. Confirmed; the height is 1,400 or about 1,800 feet on the house's own pages and is not given, as the author left it.

Native yeasts, French barrels coopered at Saint-Romain from staves air dried for about three years: Terroirsense gives François Frères barrels alone with three years of air drying, merchants hand stacked French cooperage air dried at Saint-Romain; most accounts give native yeast, but one merchant's sheet of 2012 gives indigenous and cultured yeasts and another native yeast only since 2008. Hedged as the house's account (below).

Full malolactic and long lees contact: Wine Spectator has native strains driving primary and malolactic fermentation; one account gives eleven to eighteen months on the lees; full malolactic is the library's. Stands on the library.

The move from the first winery to Vine Hill Road in the early 1990s: Chambers Wines and Wine-Searcher give a first winery at Nelligan Road, Glen Ellen, until late 1991, the new one ready for the 1992 harvest, and the Vine Hill vines planted in 1988. Confirmed.

The flagship: Vinfolio and the Ideal Wine Company call the Kistler Vineyard Chardonnay the house's flagship, with Cuvée Cathleen a selection from one of its blocks in some vintages. The plan's note is answered and the pick kept; the trap set right (below).
The rules: the founder, his partner, the winemaker from 2017 and the owners since 2008 kept out; no price, no score; British spelling; no dash. Sound.

The questions: the wine question's full malolactic and lees against Viognier, steel and dried grapes, one right answer; the story question's 1986 against 1979, 1992 and 1976, each a year of the story or near it. Sound.

tested: The founding year left empty: the accounts give a weekend hobby from 1979, a first commercial vintage of 1981 and the house's own 1978 and 1981. The empty field stands.

A garage and Zinfandel first: the PinotFile and Prince of Pinot give Zinfandel in 1979, from free grapes and from the Martinelli family, made in a garage or at the founder's house; the house says it began in a garage, at Forestville on one page and Fulton on another. Kept as the late 1970s in a garage.

Hacienda del Rio, then Williams Selyem from the 1984 vintage: Prince of Pinot and the PinotFile give the name changed after a complaint from Hacienda Winery, with the 1984 vintage the first under the new name; one account gives 1982 for the first vintage under the name and another a letter of 1983. Kept, the spread open.

The first Pinot Noir in 1982 from Rochioli: Wine Spectator gives 1982; the PinotFile and the house's own materials give Rochioli Pinot Noir first bought in 1980 and bottled under Hacienda del Rio. Set right to the early 1980s (below).

The 1985 Rochioli Vineyard Pinot Noir and the sweepstakes prize: the house's history gives 2,316 wines entered at the State Fair of 1987, its 2020 newsletter 2,136; outside accounts agree on the year. Confirmed, and the year added.

The move of 1988 into barns: the house says the grower offered space and the founders set their tanks on a concrete pad under a tin roof with the barrels in a new, bare bones building on his ranch; the PinotFile and Prince of Pinot give an introduction in 1987 and the move for the 1989 harvest or in December 1989. Set right (below).

The sale of 1998 and Faiveley's stakes: Wikipedia (from the San Francisco Chronicle of January 2021) gives the minority stake of 2021; The Drinks Business, the Press Democrat and Wine Spectator the majority of June 2024. Confirmed.
The River Block: the house's vineyard page gives clones 115, 777, East, Pommard and West Block and Yolo sandy loam, a house note the river bank and deep loam with river gravel. Confirmed.

The making: the house's history and newsletters of 2020 and 2025 give stainless steel dairy tanks as fermenters, kept for their ratio of skins to juice; the sheets for 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022 and 2024 give sixteen months in barrel, 64 to 83 per cent new and the rest one year old. Set right (below).

The rules: the founders described (one died in 2019 by the San Francisco Chronicle and Wine Spectator, the other's status not found), the owners of 1998 and the Faiveley family members kept out; the house of Faiveley named as a house. No price, no score, nothing volatile beyond ownership told with its year. Sound.

The questions: the wine question's sandy loam by the river against Mayacamas volcanic hillsides, Sonoma Coast shale and Alexander Valley gravel benches, one right answer; the story question's Rochioli against Allen, Hanzell and Seghesio. Sound once the years are set right.

changed.was: Two friends began making wine for fun in a garage in the Russian River Valley in the late 1970s, starting with Zinfandel, and sold their first wines under the name Hacienda del Rio. In 1982 they made their first Pinot Noir, from grapes grown by the Rochioli family on Westside Road, who had begun planting Pinot Noir there in 1968. The founders soon put their own surnames on the label, and the 1984 vintage was the first called Williams Selyem. A year later came the wine that made them: the 1985 Rochioli Vineyard Pinot Noir won the sweepstakes prize at the California State Fair against more than two thousand wines. Demand outran the little garage, and a waiting list to join the house's mailing list followed. In 1988, by the house's account, a Westside Road grower offered them room, and they moved into barns among the vineyards they bought from. The founders sold the house in 1998. In 2021 the Burgundy house of Faiveley took a minority stake, and in 2024 a majority. The Rochioli Riverblock is the thread back to the beginning: Rochioli fruit made the house's name, and the riverside block is where it is grown.

changed.was: Jordan began in 1972, when a couple inspired by the estates of France bought land in Alexander Valley near Healdsburg and planted Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot on the valley floor. To advise them they hired André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994), the Russian born winemaker who had shaped Beaulieu in Napa, and he set the house on a French course. Building of the château began in 1974, and its cellar was finished a week before the harvest of 1976, the first Jordan Cabernet Sauvignon, which was released in 1980. A Chardonnay followed, and the house kept to those two wines. The winemaker who made that first vintage stayed until 2019. After phylloxera in the 1990s Jordan turned to growers on the Alexander Valley benchland, whose grapes suited its style better than the valley floor. The founders' son took over the running of the house in 2005, and in 2021 it bought another Alexander Valley vineyard. Jordan Cabernet is a lesson in the balanced California Cabernet: medium bodied, aged before release and made to sit beside food rather than to overwhelm it.
changed.now: Jordan began in 1972, when a couple inspired by the estates of France bought land in Alexander Valley near Healdsburg and planted Cabernet Sauvignon and Merlot on the valley floor. To advise them they hired André Tchelistcheff (1901 to 1994), the Russian born winemaker who had shaped Beaulieu in Napa, and he set the house on a French course. Building of the château began in the mid 1970s, and its cellar was finished a week before the harvest of 1976, the first Jordan Cabernet Sauvignon, which was released in 1980. A Chardonnay followed, and the house kept to those two wines. The winemaker who made that first vintage stayed until 2019. After phylloxera struck its valley floor vines in the 1990s, Jordan turned to growers across the valley and to hillside fruit, which its winemaker found more intense, and planted hillside vines on its own estate. The founders' son took over the running of the house in 2005, and in 2021 it bought another Alexander Valley vineyard. Jordan Cabernet is a lesson in the balanced California Cabernet: medium bodied, aged before release and made to sit beside food rather than to overwhelm it.
changed.why: Two beats set right in one field: the château was begun in 1974 by the house's history and in 1975 by its château page, so the mid 1970s; and after phylloxera the house turned to growers across the valley and to hillside fruit, which its winemaker found more intense, and planted hillsides on its own estate, rather than to benchland growers alone, the growers being many of them on the valley floor near Geyserville.

tested: The founder from Piedmont in 1886 to the Italian Swiss Colony: Wine Spectator, Winegeeks and the house's legacy page. Confirmed.

The Home Ranch bought and planted to Zinfandel in 1895: the house's vineyards page gives the planting date 1895; Winegeeks and Wine Spectator the purchase of that year; some accounts give a house bought in 1893 and the land in 1895. Confirmed.

At the Colony until 1902, when his own winery was finished: North Bay Biz and Dionysus give his resignation once the winery was built in 1902; other accounts give the winery completed, the first crush or the first wines in 1902. Confirmed.

The first wines under the family name in 1983, made by the fourth generation: the house's newsletter and the Marian's Reserve page give 1983 for the first commercial release under the name, a blend of 1975 made by the third generation among them; BKWine gives the early 1980s; only vinNEBRASKA credits a fourth generation member with the first wines. Set right (below).

The cut of the early 1990s: the house's timeline and the Sonoma County Winegrowers give 1993, output cut to wines from the vineyards the family farmed and owned; Decanter the 1990s; the author's Cigar Aficionado 1994. Confirmed as the early 1990s.

The sale of 2011 to Crimson Wine Group: Decanter, Harpers and Wine Spectator. Confirmed; family members stayed on after the sale by the author's sources, and a family winemaker later left and began his own label (Press Democrat), so for a time (below).

The oldest vines near the family's Victorian house at the foot of Rattlesnake Hill: the house's September newsletter, word for word. Stands, hedged as the house's account; the lint's note on "oldest" is answered by the hedge, a claim of the house about its own vines.
The making and the barrels: the house's sheets, read by the author; this check's searches did not reach them, and the wine question's key is set to their twelve to fifteen months (below).
Petite Sirah is Durif: the Codex's own grape, region and producer records say so in the same words. Stands.
The rules: the founder and his wife described for want of dates (none found here either); the family members of 2011 and since kept out; no price, no score. Sound.
The questions: the story question's Italian Swiss Colony against Buena Vista, Inglenook and Fountaingrove, one right answer; the wine question's key now matches the sheets and the explanation. Sound.

changed.was: The founder left Piedmont for Sonoma County in 1886 to work as a winemaker at the Italian Swiss Colony. In 1895 he and his wife bought land in Alexander Valley and planted Zinfandel there, the vineyard the family calls the Home Ranch. He kept his post at the Colony until 1902, when he finished a winery of his own, and his vines came through Prohibition. For decades the family sold its wine in bulk, and only in 1983 did the fourth generation make the first wines under the Seghesio name. In the early 1990s the family cut its output sharply and turned to wines from the vineyards it farmed, Zinfandel above all. The Home Ranch Zinfandel is the wine the house builds around the vines of 1895. In 2011 the family sold the business to Crimson Wine Group, and family members stayed on in the cellar and the vineyards. For a sommelier, Home Ranch is the place to taste what an Italian family's Zinfandel planting can become over more than a century.

planWhys: williams-selyem: "begun in a garage in 1981" gives the first commercial vintage as a beginning; the accounts give a weekend hobby from 1979, and the valley's name was made by the Rochioli Pinot Noir. Offered: "Russian River Valley house begun as a weekend hobby in 1979, whose Rochioli Pinot Noir of 1985 made its name."

codexInTension: p-hanzell holdings: the Ambassador's 1953 Vineyard among the oldest Chardonnay and Pinot Noir plantings. The library is right and the author's report wrong: the block holds both (Historic Vineyard Society, Prince of Pinot, Wikipedia).

p-kistler traps: "there is no single flagship wine". Two merchants call the Kistler Vineyard the flagship; the trap may want softening to "many single vineyards". The region record's producers line gives Kistler as founded 1979, the first vintage; the house and the library give 1978.

p-williams-selyem why: "began in a Forestville garage in the early 1980s". The accounts give a hobby from 1979 and the garage at Forestville or Fulton; and its trap names the buyer of 1998, a living man. Its style line's soft whole cluster perfume and its trap on fog through the Petaluma Gap were not tested by this check.

The region record's Williams Selyem line calls it "the first cult Pinot Noir in California", a word this tab refuses; and its Seghesio line, "Healdsburg since 1895", puts in Healdsburg a vineyard of 1895 that lies in Alexander Valley, the Healdsburg winery being later.
